query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Under increasingly aggressive acidic/chloride solutions and elevated temperatures (25–150 °C), the native oxide/passive layer on Q235 steel is destabilized, initiating localized breakdown and accelerating corrosion rates, whereas under milder or lower-temperature conditions, the passive film remains more protective, slowing the onset of corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 steel (as-received) with its naturally formed but unaltered surface oxide/passive film.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the solution’s chloride concentration (e.g., 0.1–1 M NaCl or comparable acid/chloride medium) and temperature (25–150 °C) in contact with Q235 steel; perform weight-loss measurements and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) on identically prepared steel samples.
generation.conditions: Submerge each specimen in a well-controlled acidic/chloride environment at either room temperature (~25 °C) or elevated temperatures (50, 100, and up to 150 °C) for fixed intervals, holding all other factors (e.g., pH ~1–4) constant across comparison groups.
generation.structural_mediator: Stability and thickness of the native oxide/passive film on steel surfaces, which can be influenced by solution composition and temperature.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperature and increased chloride activity synergistically promote oxide breakdown and pitting initiation, reducing the overall corrosion resistance. The destabilized oxide film accelerates anodic dissolution in the harsh environment, while lower temperatures or lower chloride concentrations better preserve the protective layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the reference steel samples exposed at mild temperature and lower chloride, test samples subjected to high temperature (≥100 °C) and high chloride levels will exhibit significantly reduced charge-transfer resistance in EIS (~25–50% lower) and noticeably higher weight-loss rates (potentially doubling or more), indicating accelerated corrosion.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel tested in near-neutral solution at 25 °C with minimal chloride, displaying more stable passivation and lower mass loss rates.
generation.boundary: At temperatures beyond 150 °C or in solutions containing additional inhibitive species, the mechanism of passivation–breakdown may be altered. Other steel compositions or protective coatings would also change the corrosion response mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: Exact magnitudes of the change in corrosion rate and EIS parameters are not experimentally established for each temperature and chloride level; the synergy between temperature, pH, and chloride is complex and may cause deviations from the approximate doubling of weight-loss or the expected EIS trends.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identically polished, pre-exposed Q235 steel coupons. Immerse them in controlled acid/chloride solutions at distinct temperatures (25 °C, 50 °C, 100 °C, 150 °C) for fixed durations. Characterize each sample’s corrosion rate via weight loss and record electrochemical impedance spectra at periodic intervals. Compare results for correlation with changes in temperature and environment severity.
measurements: Weight-loss to quantify corrosion rate changes over time.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to measure changes in corrosion kinetics and passive film stability.
Open-circuit potential and potentiodynamic polarization to determine passivation dynamics.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no systematic increase in corrosion rate or decrease in polarization resistance is observed with raising temperature or chloride concentration, then the proposed oxide-layer destabilization mechanism fails, falsifying the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: To evaluate the corrosion resistance of the coatings, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and polarization curves were obtained using a CS310H potentiostat/galvanostat. A 1 mol/L NaCl solution was used as the corrosion medium. The reference electrode used was a saturated calomel electrode (SCE). The counter electrode was platinum. In this study, the samples were Φ 8 × 10 mm cylinders, and the round exposed surface was polished. The electrochemical experimental parameters are shown in Table 5. The electrochemical experiment was performed three times with nominally identical samples.

In this work, (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA were selected as the composition of coating because of its high strength and corrosion resistance in bulk state, while the corresponding properties of coating remain unknown. Therefore, (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating on the Q235 steel substrate was fabricated by using the plasma spray technique, and the microstructure evolution during preparation process, microhardness, and corrosion behavior in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution were investigated. Furthermore, the phase formation and the corrosion behavior of the coatings were specifically analyzed.
